chapters.question: Every discovery begins with a question

hero.title: Explore the universe. Discover what changes.
hero.lead: An interactive scientific platform to explore real SPHEREx observations and investigate the dynamic universe.
hero.disclaimer: Planet and orbits are an illustration. Every number on this page is either sourced or labelled as simulated.

explore.title: Every region of the sky tells a story.
explore.body: Point at any patch of sky by its coordinates — right ascension and declination — and The Origin Project asks the SPHEREx archive what it saw there, and when.

grid.detail: The coordinate system astronomers use to address any point on the sky.

constellations.detail: Landmarks for orientation: Orion, Ursa Major, Cassiopeia and Crux.

markers.detail: The five challenge targets, placed at their catalogue positions.

mission.title: The power of SPHEREx
mission.body: NASA's SPHEREx observatory photographs the entire sky again and again, splitting its light into colours we cannot see. Each repeat is a new chance to notice what moved or changed.

bands.label: spectral bands, from six detector arrays of 17 channels each

range.label: near-infrared, beyond what the human eye can see

cadence.label: to map the whole sky, repeated since May 2025

mission.bandsPrompt: Move across the bands to see what each part of the spectrum reveals.
mission.disclaimer: The glowing strips on the sphere illustrate an all-sky survey filling in over time. They are not SPHEREx's real pointing schedule.

bands.note: Ranges per detector array, as published by NASA/IPAC IRSA. Bar heights are decorative.

a6.f2: Cold brown dwarfs glow brightest here

epochs.title: The universe changes. We help you investigate.
epochs.body: The same patch of sky, seen at different times. One star drifts, another brightens. Drag through the epochs, then switch on the difference view to keep only what changed.
epochs.why: Why compare epochs? A SPHEREx pixel spans about 6″ of sky, and the challenge's moving targets drift roughly 5–10″ per year: often less than a pixel between visits. Seeing them takes aligned frames on one shared brightness scale.

objects.title: Objects worth exploring
objects.body: The challenge names five test targets: three that move across the sky and two whose light changes. Choose one to turn the sky towards it.
objects.auditNote: Archive coverage from the project's data audit (11 Nov 2026). No variation has been measured by the platform yet; sequences for this target are being validated.

barnard.summary: A red dwarf about 6 light-years away, with the largest proper motion of any known star.
barnard.note: Expected shift across the span: up to 1.9 SPHEREx pixels.

epsindi.summary: Two brown dwarfs orbiting each other, both bound to the nearby star Epsilon Indi A.
epsindi.note: Expected shift across the span: up to 1.1 SPHEREx pixels.

wise0855.summary: The coldest brown dwarf known. Faint in the near-infrared, so a single frame may not show it.
wise0855.note: Expected shift across the span: up to 1.35 SPHEREx pixels.

rwaur.summary: A young star system still surrounded by gas and dust, known for irregular changes in brightness.
rwaur.note: Brightness comparisons need one shared intensity scale across frames.

rdra.summary: A pulsating red giant whose brightness rises and falls over a cycle of months.
rdra.note: Spread across three archive collections (qr2, qr2_deep, qr3_deep).

pipeline.title: From observation to evidence
pipeline.note: Diagrams explain each step; they are not real data. “Available” means usable in the app today. “Being validated” means built and still being checked against real SPHEREx data.

region.title: Select a region of the sky
region.detail: Search an object by name or type its RA/Dec. The sky view centres on it.

query.title: Retrieve astronomical observations
query.detail: The platform asks NASA/IPAC IRSA which SPHEREx exposures cover that point.

fits.title: Process FITS data
fits.detail: Each exposure is cut around the target and bad pixels are masked. A shared brightness scale across frames is still in development.

epochs.title: Compare different epochs
epochs.detail: Frames from the same band play in order, side by side or blinking, so change is visible to the eye.

variation.title: Analyze possible variations
variation.detail: Aligned differences point to what moved or changed. They assist your eye; they never replace it.

journal.title: Generate reproducible evidence
journal.detail: Save the target, query and frames to your journal so anyone can repeat the investigation.

visual.cutout: cutout around the target, bad pixels masked
visual.differenceMap: difference map: cyan gained light, violet lost light

platform.title: Explore the origin
platform.body: Six tools, one investigation. Each is a real part of the platform you can open right now.
platform.previewNote: The live preview loads the running application itself, not a mock-up.

observatory.name: Observatory
observatory.purpose: Start here: a live sky, a search box and the real status of the data sources.

livingSky.name: Living Sky
livingSky.purpose: Navigate the celestial sphere and see which archive exposures cover each region.

timeExplorer.name: Time Explorer
timeExplorer.purpose: Step through real epochs, compare A/B frames and run aligned differences.

spectralLab.name: Spectral Lab
spectralLab.purpose: Measured spectral profiles only. No curve is drawn without real samples.

discoveries.name: Discoveries
discoveries.purpose: Track possible candidates. Every row links back to its job and observations.

journal.name: Journal
journal.purpose: Save reproducible investigations and export the evidence.

finale.title: Every discovery begins with a question.
